nodes.name: Ag nanoparticle electrode preparation
nodes.procedure: Commercial Ag nanoparticles (99.99% APS 20-40 nm, Alfa Aesar) were dispersed in 2-propanol (99.8%, Samchun Chemicals) with Nafion resin solution (5 wt% in a mixture of lower aliphatic alcohol, Sigma-Aldrich) to prepare a catalyst ink. The ink composition was 30 mg of Ag nanoparticles and 1 mL of 2-propanol with 32 μL of Nafion resin solution. The catalyst ink was then spray coated on a gas diffusion substrate (Sigracet 39 BB, active area of 10 cm²) with a loading amount of 1 mg cm⁻².

A catalyst ink was prepared by dispersing the catalyst in 2-propanol (99.8%, Samchun Chemicals) with Nafion resin solution (5 wt% in a mixture of lower aliphatic alcohol, Sigma-Aldrich)... (ii) 30 mg of Ag nanoparticles and 1 mL of 2-propanol with 32 μL of Nafion resin solution for the Ag electrode. The loading amount of the catalyst was set as 1 mg cm⁻² for both types of electrodes.

nodes.name: Ni-N/C electrode preparation
nodes.procedure: Ni-N/C was synthesized by a method described in a previous report. A catalyst ink was prepared by dispersing 100 mg of Ni-N/C in 10 mL of 2-propanol (99.8%, Samchun Chemicals) with 120 μL of Nafion resin solution (5 wt% in a mixture of lower aliphatic alcohol, Sigma-Aldrich). The catalyst ink was then spray coated on a gas diffusion substrate (Sigracet 39 BB, active area of 10 cm²) with a loading amount of 1 mg cm⁻².

nodes.name: IrO2 anode electrode preparation
nodes.procedure: IrO2 (99.9%, Alfa Aesar) was dispersed in 1 mL of 2-propanol (99.8%, Samchun Chemicals) with 34.1 μL of Nafion resin solution (5 wt% in a mixture of lower aliphatic alcohol, Sigma-Aldrich) to prepare a catalyst ink. The ink composition was 30 mg of IrO2 in 1 mL of 2-propanol with 34.1 μL of Nafion solution. The catalyst ink was then spray coated on a gas diffusion substrate (Sigracet 39 BB, active area of 10 cm²) with a loading amount of 1 mg cm⁻².

nodes.name: MEA electrolyzer assembly
nodes.procedure: An MEA-type CO2 electrolyzer (10 cm² scale, CNL) was assembled with zero gap by placing either an anion exchange membrane (AEM) (Sustainion X37-50 grade T, Dioxide Materials) or PVDF porous membrane (0.45 μm of pore size, Merck) between the cathode (Ag electrode or Ni-N/C electrode) and anode (IrO2 electrode). Humidified CO2 gas was supplied to the cathode part at a rate of 225 mL min⁻¹. At the anode, a 1 M KHCO3 (Sigma-Aldrich) electrolyte was circulated by a peristaltic pump.

nodes.description: CO2 reduction reaction performance at -3.0 V with anion exchange membrane
nodes.source_text: One sequence comprised a single chronoamperometry (i.e., current-time curve at a constant voltage of -3.0, -3.2, or -3.4 V) integrated with the measurement of online GC and subsequent LSV (current-voltage curve) under CO2 feed, which, respectively, provided the CO2RR performance and electrochemical activity trend on the postreaction catalyst. Every 72nd cycle, LSV was performed under an inert N2 feed to observe only the HER activity on the catalyst.

nodes.description: CO2 reduction reaction performance at -3.4 V with PVDF porous membrane for extrapolation validation
nodes.source_text: We collected LSV data at -3.4 V using Zn, known for CO production, and employed the data to evaluate the extrapolation of our model. We utilized the early stage degradation data of the Zn catalyst, where FECO is high because HCOOH has not been produced yet, to ensure data consistency with our training data. Notably, for the Zn -3.4 V data, which was not included in the training set, our model accurately predicted all three targets.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM imaging at 10 kV accelerating voltage reveals surface morphology of Ag nanoparticles and Ni-N/C electrodes. Ag samples show potassium impurity deposition that becomes more severe with degradation, while Ni-N/C shows agglomeration of single atoms into nanoparticles.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Surface morphology of Ag nanoparticles and Ni-N/C electrodes was, respectively, observed by SEM (InspectF50, FEI) at an accelerating voltage of 10 kV ... potassium impurities (derived from the 1 M KHCO₃ electrolyte) covered the Ag nanoparticles in the moderate FE_CO sample, and this phenomenon became more severe in the low FE_CO sample.

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM at 200 kV accelerating voltage shows atomically dispersed Ni single atoms in high FE_CO samples that disappear and agglomerate into Ni nanoparticles in moderate and low FE_CO samples, indicating active site loss during degradation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in STEM images, the atomically dispersed Ni single atoms observed on the high FE_CO sample disappear and further agglomerate into Ni nanoparticles for moderate and low FE_CO samples.

properties.description: High-resolution TEM micrographs showing nanostructure morphology

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS analysis of Ag 3d and K 2p peaks shows no significant change in Ag oxidation state across degradation stages, but reveals potassium deposition on the catalyst surface. XPS-N 1s analysis of Ni-N/C shows decreased relative peak area for Ni-N species in degraded samples.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The chemical state of Ag nanoparticles and Ni-N/C electrodes was analyzed by XPS (Nexsa, Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a monochromated Al-K alpha (1486.6 eV) source ... the particle size (Figure 5a) and oxidation state of Ag (Figure 5b) were not significantly different ... XPS-N 1s deconvolution analysis also suggested that the relative peak area for Ni-N species decreased for moderate and low FE_CO samples.

nodes.characterization_summary: EXAFS analysis of Ni K-edge shows disappearance of initial Ni-N bond and appearance of new Ni-Ni peak during long-term stability testing, confirming Ni single atom dissolution and redeposition as Ni nanoparticles.
nodes.evidence_snippet: During the long-term stability tests, the initial Ni-N bond disappeared and a new Ni-Ni peak appeared.

properties.description: Multiple spectra showing coordination environment analysis

nodes.characterization_summary: Linear sweep voltammetry under CO₂ and N₂ feed shows progressive changes in electrochemical behavior during catalyst degradation. The difference between CO₂ and N₂ LSV curves decreases as degradation proceeds, indicating loss of CO₂RR performance. LSV curves serve as input descriptor for machine learning model predicting catalytic performance.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In practice, the difference between CO₂ and N₂ LSV curves in negative voltage regions decreases as the cycle progresses and becomes nearly negligible in the later stage of the experiments indicating the loss of CO₂RR performance.

properties.description: Current measurement from linear sweep voltammetry

nodes.characterization_summary: Grad-CAM interpretation of the CNN model reveals that Ag degradation is primarily governed by extrinsic factors (mass transport limitations in the diffusion-limited region around -3.2 V), while Ni-N/C degradation is governed by intrinsic kinetic factors (active site loss).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The high importance scores are predominantly concentrated on the negative voltage region at approximately -3.2 V, where the extrinsic factors of reaction can primarily affect performance. Thus, it is suggested that understanding the behavior of CO₂RR on Ag is mainly determined by the extrinsic properties of Ag instead of by the intrinsic properties.

nodes.characterization_summary: Tafel plots derived from LSV curves show two distinct regions: kinetic region and diffusion-limited region. For Ag, the transition point remains relatively stable, while for Ni-N/C, the transition point shifts toward more negative voltages with degradation, and the Tafel slope increases significantly.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 4c illustrates the obtained Tafel plots from the conducted experiments, comprising two distinct regions: a kinetic region and a diffusion-limited region ... As in Figure 4f region (1), strong attention can be observed in the intermediate voltage region. Notably, the attention is focused in the vicinity of the transition points and distributed broadly.

nodes.characterization_summary: First derivative of LSV curves (dLSV) identifies transition points between kinetic and diffusion-limited regions. For Ag, the transition point shifts toward more negative voltages as FE_CO decreases. For Ni-N/C, the transition point becomes less distinct and ultimately disappears in advanced degradation stages.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The transition point where the reaction-rate governing factor changes from intrinsic kinetic to extrinsic properties can be readily determined from the dLSV curve.
